eligibility_reason: A pre-registered Registered Report (Results Blind track) that collects new data from 62 musicians and 62 non-musicians to replicate Proverbio et al. (2016, Sci. Rep.), which claimed skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect; results are reported in full.

effects.original_title: Skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect
effects.original_authors: Proverbio, A.; Massetti, G.; Rizzi, E.; Zani, A.
effects.outcome: McGurk effect in skilled musicians: accuracy of consonant identification for audiovisual incongruent (McGurk) stimuli versus audio-only stimuli, and its size relative to non-musicians
effects.contrast: audio-only vs audiovisual incongruent stimuli within musicians (and the condition x group interaction, musicians vs non-musicians)
effects.description: Skilled musicians (unlike non-musicians) are not subject to the McGurk effect: their consonant identification is not reduced when the auditory syllable is dubbed onto a video of a different articulation.
effects.citation_sentence: Proverbio and colleagues [2] argue that the McGurk effect is absent in highly trained musicians. ... For these reasons, it is valuable to conduct a close replication of this study to assess whether skilled musicians really are not subject to the McGurk effect. [ref 2: Proverbio A, Massetti G, Rizzi E, Zani A. 2016. Skilled musicians are not subject to the McGurk effect. Sci. Rep. 6, 30423]
effects.evidence: Results 3.1 (replication analysis): 'The statistical analysis confirmed that musicians have a highly significant McGurk effect (b = -2.34, z = -18.37, p < 0.001) ... musicians' McGurk effect was in fact significantly larger than the non-musicians' McGurk effect (b = 0.46, z = 2.72, p = 0.007)'; same in targeted analysis 3.2. Abstract: 'Contrary to the original study's conclusion, we find that musicians do show a large and statistically significant McGurk effect and that their effect is no smaller than that of non-musicians.' Conclusion: 'musicians are subject to the McGurk effect, and to at least as much extent (if not more) as non-musicians are.'
effects.notes: Original claimed an ABSENCE of the McGurk effect in musicians (a null claim); the replication finds a large significant effect, so per the null-claim rule this is failure. Enumeration: the paper tests two hypotheses (musicians' McGurk effect > 0; musicians' effect smaller than non-musicians') and runs two analyses (replication coding and targeted place-of-articulation coding) on the same participants. I treat these as tests/analysis paths of ONE original claim (the abstract frames them as two readings of the single claim 'skilled musicians are not subject to' the effect); a second coder could split into two entries (no-effect claim -> failure; smaller-than-non-musicians claim -> failure, arguably reversal since musicians' effect was significantly larger, but the original's group difference was non-significant and the authors say the larger effect 'should be interpreted with caution', so not reversal). Both analyses agree, so no inconclusive. Type: authors call it a 'close replication'; methodology changed (within- vs between-participants manipulation, doubled N, GLMM instead of ANOVA, noisier stimuli, extra targeted coding) AND context changed (Mandarin/Cantonese speakers in Hong Kong/Shenzhen vs Italian participants), so close extension per tiebreaker; close experiment is a plausible alternative since the authors list language as a 'minor difference'. Original authors' full first names not given in the paper (initials only). Stage 1 accepted via Results Blind track (submitted after data collection).
